stories.headline: Mets, A.J. Ewing reach 8-year, $95M extension, sources say
stories.summary: The Mets and 22-year-old center fielder A.J. Ewing have agreed to an eight-year, $95 million contract extension, sources confirmed to ESPN.
stories.body:
The New York Mets and center fielder A.J. Ewing are in agreement on an eight-year, $95 million contract extension that includes a club option for a ninth season, sources confirmed to ESPN's Jeff Passan on Saturday.

The deal buys out Ewing's two remaining pre-arbitration years, his three arbitration years and at least three free agent years. It is pending a physical.

Ewing's deal is the largest contract extension for a pre-arbitration player in franchise history. David Wright -- arguably the greatest position player in Mets history -- previously held the mark with a six-year, $55 million deal he signed in August 2006.

Ewing, 22, was selected by the Mets in the fourth round of the 2023 draft out of high school. The Ohio native made his major league debut in May and was one of the few bright spots in another disappointing season in Queens.

While concluding his rookie season as a below-average hitter -- he posted a 97 wRC+ -- he showed flashes as a future leadoff hitter and supplied plus baserunning and elite defense at a premium position.

After a hot start to his career, Ewing recovered from a deep midseason slump to slash .318/.390/.489 over his last 25 games. He finished with a .252 batting average, 11 home runs, 25 steals and a .700 OPS in 120 games. The total package produced a 2.0 fWAR.

The Mets' outfield appears to be set for years to come with Ewing in center, fellow rookie Carson Benge in right and franchise cornerstone Juan Soto in left. Benge, another elite defender, was also part of the Mets' silver lining in 2026, finishing second in National League Rookie of the Year voting after batting .282 with 20 home runs, 22 steals and a .776 OPS in 156 games.

SNY first reported news of the deal.

stories.headline: AFL Draft 2026: Grading the draft hauls for every club
stories.summary: The 2026 AFL Draft has been run, but which team won? ESPN's draft expert Jasper Chellappah has handed down five As and two Ds after this year's two-night affair.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL Draft has been run and done, so let's get into grading each team's haul. Night one was headlined by a Brisbane points matching debacle, with the Swans landing Caylen Murray.

It flipped the script for teams down the order with the Saints and Pies landing their preferred prospects thanks to Brisbane's three-point miss on Murray.

On night two there was a clear directive from clubs to draft based on list need. With the crop of talent 15 past 40 so even this year, clubs were focused on specific roles that suit the modern game and it resulted in bolting mature-agers earning main list opportunities.

These draft grades aren't just based on the calibre of talent brought into the club - it was a lot easier for Port Adelaide and Carlton to land star youngsters than North Melbourne and Geelong. It takes into account live trading, value on each pick and positional fits at the club.

These are ESPN's draft grades for every club after the 2026 AFL Draft.

READ: 'No one saw it coming' - Inside the Swans' draft heist that landed a Lions Academy star

Adelaide
Pre-draft hand: 15, 32, 35, 43, 54

Selections: Toby Krasna (14), Xavier Ladbrook (34), Sam Tassone (44)
There was a clear plan from the Crows to address their transition ball movement, and they've done so here. Krasna is an outside midfielder that really came on this year with his class in space. He runs hard both ways, plays with flair on the ball and is incisive with his foot skills in the forward half.

Xavier Ladbrook will take time to develop as a 202cm key defender that needs time in the gym, but his running base and length gives him an exciting platform. It was rounded out with local dasher Sam Tassone who has some raw, developable traits with speed out of defence.

The Crows passed up Anthony Long after Geelong's bid on the NGA forward.

Grade: B-

Brisbane
Pre-draft hand: 21, 27, 28, 45

Selections: Kodah Edwards (27), Archie Van Dyk (28), Jackson Phillips (29), Archie Spencer (36)

We haven't seen a bid matching debacle quite like Brisbane's on night one when they fell three points short of keeping Caylen Murray. The Lions cornered themselves and found no trade partner on the clock.

It meant they unexpectedly carried three selections back to back early on night two, opting for two South Adelaide products in Edwards and Van Dyke as they addressed their midfield mix.

Edwards captained SA and has versatility to play on-ball or through the forward 50, while Van Dyk has the size and skill to develop rapidly in a professional environment.

Phillips looks a natural wingman at the next level with good ball use off both feet and disciplined running patterns. He looks most likely to play senior football early next year, and they rounded out with dashing defender Archie Spencer.

Grade: D

Carlton
Pre-draft hand: 13, 18, 31, 50, 59, 67, 73

Selections: Cody Walker (3), Harvey Spawton-Guy (32), Jackson Watkins (37), Ethan Herbert (46)

A nice mix of prospects for the Blues began with the arrival of Cody Walker early on night one. The gifted midfielder has Brownlow upside in his prime as a natural ball-winner that puts speed on the game with aggressive movement.

WA's Harvey Spawton-Guy will be looked at as a tall to develop at both ends of the ground - he competes superbly in the air and that attack on the footy bodes well. Jackson Watkins plays with power in the forward half as a smaller type and Ethan Herbert's upside as a ruck of the future is enticing with his ball-winning and skill around the ground a point of difference.

Grade: A-

Collingwood
Pre-draft hand: 11, 30, 63, 64, 65

Selections: Sam Gayfer (12), Gus Kennedy (31), Jordan Knapp (41), Koby LeCras (62)

This is some sort of result for the Pies. They had Gayfer circled on their board from a long way out and were delighted to find him available. His courage and strength in the air at a combine-record vertical leap will be a nightmare to defend.

Kennedy is one of the great characters of the class and plays with a lot of energy off halfback, while Knapp is an exceptional ball magnet through the midfield but will need to build size at the next level.

Rounding out a significant haul was one of the big sliders Koby LeCras. The nephew of premiership Eagle Mark, the 192cm forward can roam up wings with a big engine and is a beautiful kick around goals off his preferred left.

Grade: A

Essendon
Pre-draft hand: 1, 17, 25, 69, 75, 78, 80 (plus second round compensation pick)

Selections: Ethan Drever (2), Archie Elliott (17), Harvie Cooke (21), Jack Pickett (26), Blake Justice (55)

The Bombers had a lot of work to do on each night and they will come away happy with the draft haul. Drever is the perfect complement to previous drafts through the midfield as the outside speed and damage, rating him as the No. 1 player in the open pool.

They paired him with best mate Archie Elliott which produced the best moment of night one as he was pulled out of the crowd at Marvel Stadium. The small forward is an excellent aerialist and has a defensive edge to his game that appeals.

Harvie Cooke was the Talent League's best and fairest and will suit a high half forward role at the next level, while the 194cm Jack Pickett is the big upside swing in the second round as the most accurate set shot to come through the pathways in some time. He will take time as he rehabs a torn ACL and MCL.

The Dons rounded it out with NGA Blake Justice who will be a slow starter to pre-season with a hamstring, but the 192cm midfielder has a unique blend of speed, agility and height that is exciting to develop.

Grade: B+

Fremantle
Pre-draft hand: 19, 40, 58, 61, 68

Selections: George Dimer (18), Kane Johnston (42), Jake Medved (57)

The Dockers have some ready-made options to add depth on a flag tilt. They were delighted that Dimer got through a host of suitors late on night one, and he looms as an immediate Switkowski replacement. Dimer is ultra-clean below his knees at 173cm and sets up teammates selflessly.

Kane Johnston is a 24-year-old tall out of the WAFL that's played his best footy in the forward 50 but could be utilised in defence. His body is ready to compete and the athleticism is AFL level.

Fremantle pinched Jake Medved out of the Swans Academy to round out their night. The utility has played in just about every position this season but could be best used as a wingman with his ranginess and endurance base.

Grade: C+

Geelong
Pre-draft hand: 36, 55, 60

Selections: Lachie Hicks (38), Anthony Long (56), Zach Stevens (60)

This was a quintessential Cats draft. They entered late on night two and immediately took a swing on one of the best athletes in the draft. Hicks has the speed-endurance blend Geelong covets, covering big distances and racking up the ball all season for the Western Jets.

Anthony Long was one of five(!) academy prospects they bid on late. The Crows NGA prospect is Izak Rankine's cousin and brings sharp agility and forward 50 creativity at 184cm.

Finally, Zach Stevens was the classic local product pick out of South Barwon. He's possibly the fastest product to be drafted and as a half forward showed flashes in the VFL and at Talent League levels.

Grade: B

Gold Coast
Pre-draft hand: 8, 70, 72, 77

Selections: Leo Steed (10), Elliott Himmelberg (63), Jamarra Ugle-Hagan (64)

The Suns took one live pick to the draft via Ben King's compensation. They opted for the midfield option in WA's Leo Steed, whose clean hands, strong transition running and fantastic work ethic rocketed his stocks this year. Steed has balance and selflessness to his game.

They rounded out the draft with two rookie elevations.

Grade: C

GWS
Pre-draft hand: 9, 20, 26, 57

Selections: Ethan Matthews (6), Jake Eime (13), Andrio Sousa (45)

Matthews is the best academy prospect GWS has had since Tom Green, and the earliest they've ever taken in a draft. The Giants moved up as far as they could so their residual draft pick would sit in the teens and with that pick they opted for Jake Eime.

A very Giants-esque selection, the SA product is an aggressive rebounder off halfback with the dare to tuck the ball and take on opponents. He can finish off transition in the forward half with good disposal and forms an exciting combination with Lachie Ash.

On night two Andrio Sousa presented as a fantastic athlete to develop on a wing or forward flank, though in isolation trading pick 20 to the Power for a future second-rounder was a poor return.

Grade: B-

Hawthorn
Pre-draft hand: 29, 37, 66, 74

Selections: Benji Van Rooyen (30), Cooper Hodge (58), Keenan Boi (59)

The Hawks targeted a real list need with Van Rooyen, the younger brother of Melbourne's Jacob. He's a legitimate ruck size and uses his physicality in the air well, enjoying the best championships of any ruck this year playing for WA.

The Cats made sneaky bids on Luke's son Cooper Hodge and Keenan Boi, with the latter sliding through to make for a comfortable bid match. Hodge's best traits come in the contest where he's tough and aggressive, while Boi has a lot of power in the forward half.

Grade: C+

Melbourne
Pre-draft hand: 4, 14, 48, 51, 79

Selections: Mitch Harris (7), Lochie Burrows (15), Ben Forster (49), Kaie Sullivan (52)

The Dees had another two first-rounders to play with and opted for the top key defender in Harris. His form a SANFL League level to finish the season cemented his top-10 status and Melbourne will look to him and Disco Turner as the future combination in defence.

Lochie Burrows is one of the best characters in the draft and gives the Dees huge flexibility as a halfback or hard-nosed on-baller. Ben Forster is a role player swing late in the draft with the wingman running hard both ways and offering neat skills in space. Kaie Sullivan was the late-season boater out of the Stingrays after a huge finals campaign elevated his stock off half forward.

Grade: B

North Melbourne
Pre-draft hand: 33, 49, 62

Selections: George Gale (23), Seb Marsic (35), Aidan McCartney (54)

The Roos traded their future first-rounder to get in for George Gale, such was their plaudits of the hardened youngster. He runs hard as an outside midfielder and has the size to eventually transition inside, but looks like a disciplined role player that will allow others to shine early in his career.

Seb Marsic was a bolter on night two as a big, physical key forward. He kicked seven goals in a game that North's Ollie Griffin kicked four at the other end.

The Aidan McCartney bid was matched late on night two with the 195cm son of Jason finding his way to Arden St.

Grade: B-

Port Adelaide
Pre-draft hand: 7, 12, 22, 24, 34, 46

Selections: Dougie Cochrane (1), Clancy Snell (19), Wil Malady (20), Wil Antrobus (25), Gabriel Patterson (39), Angus White (47)

The draft of the year goes to Port Adelaide. Dougie Cochrane was only the start for them, but it was a big one with the consensus best prospect in the pool becoming Port's first-ever No. 1 pick.

Shrewd live trading landed picks 19 and 20 and they grabbed sliders. Clancy Snell is one of the best interceptors in the crop and at 197cm will play on a range of forwards. Wil Malady is an upside swing on the clear talent. The 190cm forward is athletic and brilliant in the air.

Wil Antrobus was an early call at pick 25 but fits a clear need out of defence. His left leg is lethal in open play and he can be relied upon to kick in. They finished off with local products - Gabe Patterson plays with power in the forward half while Angus White has rehabbed an ACL this year but adds speed through the midfield.

Grade: A+

Richmond
Pre-draft hand: 2, 5, 44, 76 (plus second round compensation pick)

Selections: Arki Butler (4), Harry Van Hattum (8), Noah Williams (22), Harry Franz (51)

Richmond landed open prospects at 1 and 3 in ESPN's Power Rankings. Arki Butler, the match-winning medium forward, and Harry Van Hattum, the standout ruckman, are upside swings into the future. Neither can be expected to hit the ground running fully next year but could spearhead the Tigers into a new era.

Noah Williams was a smart choice at 22 with his competitiveness through the midfield and in defence giving him the versatility to play early. Richmond finished their draft with Harry Franz, a high-flying 194cm defender out of SA that plays with physicality.

Grade: A+

St Kilda
Pre-draft hand: 10, 16, 41

Selections: Gustavo Teixeira (11), Tyson Bradley (16), Lewis Houndsome (43)

The Saints could not believe their luck when Brisbane didn't match on Caylen Murray and Gus Teixeira slid all the way through to 11. A genuine first overall pick chance at stages this year, Teixeira has power, class and upside in the forward half.

They nabbed another bayside product at 16 in Vic Metro MVP Tyson Bradley. At 195cm he should grow into the physical key defender that takes on the big forwards at AFL level.

St Kilda finished off night two with Lewis Houndsome, a big key forward that's played well through the ruck but struggled with injuries after a promising bottom-age campaign.

Grade: A

Sydney
Pre-draft hand: 6, 38, 39, 47

Selections: Caylen Murray (9), Brady Wright (40), Mitch Knevitt (48), Mason McGroder (61)

It was a bold and brilliant coup to land Murray, but it remains to be seen if he was best available for the Swans at that point. It's a clear list need with the departure of Nick Blakey in the off-season; Murray offers dash and class off halfback, being one of the most reliable distributors in the crop and offering midfield upside.

Brady Wright was prolific for Werribee in the VFL, and the 194cm goalkicker is a best 23 candidate next year after winning the Fothergill-Round-Mitchell Medal. They added to their mature-age pickups with delisted Cat Mitch Knevitt, whose size around the ball could prove valuable.

Mason McGroder didn't attract a bid until pick 61 which made matching a formality. The long jumper won silver at the U20s World Games in Oregon this year and presents as one of the best athletes to ever come into the AFL system.

Grade: B+

West Coast
Pre-draft hand: 3, 23, 56 (plus second round compensation pick)

Selections: Heath Mellody (5), Jake Soutar (24), Harper Banfield (65)

The pickups are solid for the Eagles, but the way they approached this draft is up for debate for a second straight year. Despite being armed with more list spots than any team in the competition thanks to assistance packages, they were once again caught out this week, not turning over enough primary list spots.

West Coast traded a valuable second-rounder into next year, receiving North's future first in the heavily-compromised 2027 draft -- Tasmania's first. As a result they only took the three picks this time around -- a disappointment for a rebuilding side -- all from WA.

Heath Mellody is the best WA prospect since Luke Jackson, providing the outside run and carry that clubs covet. He's an elite kick and fits alongside Harley Reid and Willem Duursma superbly. Jake Soutar is the readymade option and they went early on the 20-year-old. He's a natural interceptor at 190cm and will likely play on third talls next year.

They rounded out the night by taking father-son Harper Banfield with their natural selection after a bid didn't materialise. He's a strong-bodied midfielder with an elite endurance base.

Grade: D+

Western Bulldogs
Pre-draft hand: 42, 52, 53, 71

Selections: Khaled El Souki (33), Jack Riding (50), Sam Devers (53)

It was an uncomfortable wait through night one and early parts of night two for a bid on El Souki to arrive. The small forward NGA landed in an ideal part of the draft for the Dogs to match and the eruption from El Souki's family and friends was worth the wait. His physicality, left foot and goal sense gives him an elite platform to blossom at the Dogs.

The 26-year-old Jack Riding has toiled away with Werribee to earn this opportunity, and is drafted with a role for him in the forward 50. He's a beautiful crumber of the ball and has mixed it in senior football already.

Sam Devers is an upside play as a 189cm defender that straight lines the ball and puts speed on the game. He took time returning this year after a shoulder reconstruction.

Grade: B

stories.headline: Tom Brady tops list of athletes who became owners
stories.summary: The legendary quarterback is a member of an exclusive list of athletes that includes LeBron James, Serena Williams and Wayne Gretzky.
stories.body:
Tom Brady is getting (back) into the ownership game.

On Friday, sources confirmed to ESPN and NFL Network that the former superstar quarterback had bought shares in the English soccer giants Chelsea. Brady's purchasing of Chelsea shares comes after he departed the ownership group of another English club, EFL Championship side Birmingham City, earlier in the month after originally becoming a minority owner with a 3.3% stake.

Brady's latest interest isn't his only foray into the world of ownership -- he also owns a 5% minority stake in the Las Vegas Raiders, purchased in 2024, and he also has a stake in the Las Vegas Aces.

The NFL legend is far from the first athlete, active or former, to enter the ownership sphere. Here are other athletes who are now team owners:

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Atlético Madrid

In October 26 news broke that the star Oklahoma City Thunder guard would be joining the club as an investor.

"I am excited to officially join the group of shareholders of Atlético de Madrid," Gilgeous-Alexander said in the club's post. "This is a club with a long history at the top of European football, and I am grateful for the opportunity to be part of its future."

Jason Kidd -- Everton

In April 2025, English Premier League club Everton announced that then-Dallas Mavericks coach Jason Kidd would be adding a different title to his résumé: ownership group member. The news came after Kidd joined Roundhouse Capital Holdings, which is part of the Friedkin Group -- the U.S. firm that completed its takeover of Everton's ownership the previous December.

Vince Carter, Tracy McGrady, Jozy Altidore -- Buffalo Bills

In December 2024, the Bills announced Carter, McGrady and Altidore were among 10 limited partners the team was adding to its ownership group. Both McGrady (New York Knicks) and Altidore (New York Red Bulls) played for New York-area teams, while Carter spent time with the Brooklyn Nets (who were known as the New Jersey Nets at the time) and was McGrady's teammate on the Toronto Raptors (who are closer to Buffalo than NYC-based teams).

Tom Brady -- Las Vegas Aces, Las Vegas Raiders, Chelsea

The Las Vegas Aces, the reigning WNBA champions, have added to their championship credentials. Seven-time Super Bowl champion Tom Brady acquired a minority stake in the team whose majority owner is Las Vegas Raiders owner Mark Davis.

"I have always been a huge fan of women's sports, and I admire the work that the Aces' players, staff, and the WNBA continue to do to grow the sport and empower future generations of athletes," Brady said in a statement. "To be able to contribute in any way to that mission as a member of the Aces organization is an incredible honor."

Brady attended an Aces game in May 2022 and sent gifts to star Kelsey Plum. Plum and other Aces players were excited to have Brady as part of the team.

He also added the Las Vegas Raiders to his resume after his purchase of minority stake in the franchise was approved by NFL teams owners on Tuesday. The deal was agreed on in May 2023, but it took owners 17 months to give their approval over concerns he was receiving too much of a discount from majority owner Mark Davis.

Brady was also a minority owner of Birmingham City, a club in English soccer's second-tier Championship, but sold his shares in November 2026. He purchased shares in Chelsea later that month.

Lewis Hamilton -- Denver Broncos

The Broncos' ownership group added racing royalty in August 2022. Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton has a stake with the Walton-Penner group, which purchased the team in June 2022.

Hamilton, 37, has the Formula One record for most race wins and has won the Formula One title seven times. The ownership group, which purchased the team for $4.65 billion, is led by Walmart heir Rob Walton and includes former U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, who also has a stake.

In April, Hamilton joined with Serena Williams in a consortium led by former Liverpool chairman Martin Broughton in an attempt to buy Premier League club Chelsea.

"He is a champion competitor who knows what it takes to lead a winning team," Walton said in a statement.

Marshawn Lynch -- Seattle Kraken

Lynch spent 13 seasons in Seattle with the Seahawks, but his new sports venture in the state of Washington is on the ice. On April 18, he joined the Seattle Kraken ownership team as a minority investor. The former NFL running back will be a part of the NHL's "Hockey is for Everyone" campaign and Kraken owner Tod Leiweke said Lynch expressed interest in shadowing him to learn hockey CEO operations.

"This is something I never would have imagined," Lynch said to CNBC in a statement. "I always dreamed of playing on a professional team but owning one is something special. As I look back on some of my accomplishments...I'm [going to] continue to count my blessings."

Grammy Award-winning artist and Seattle native Macklemore also joined the Kraken ownership team with Lynch.

Wayne Gretzky, Steve Nash and Dustin Johnson -- Las Vegas Desert Dogs

Wayne Gretzky is a big lacrosse guy? Yep, you read that right. The Great One may have made his name on the ice, but before Gretzky was the pride of the Edmonton Oilers he was a bona fide lax bro.

"The national sport of Canada is box lacrosse," Gretzky said. "I started playing lacrosse on a team at the age of six and played all the way until I was 16 years old. I have a great love for the game in the sense I really think that box lacrosse was such a crucial part of the success I ultimately had in ice hockey."

Because of this, it shouldn't be completely surprising that the hockey legend is linking up with 2020 Masters champion Dustin Johnson, NBA Hall of Famer and current Brooklyn Nets head coach Steve Nash and Nets owner Joe Tsai as part of a star-studded ownership group for the National Lacrosse League's newest expansion team in Las Vegas, the Desert Dogs.

Dwyane Wade -- Utah Jazz

Seeing Dwyane Wade support any team other than the Miami Heat is decidedly jarring. In April, the three-time NBA champion purchased an ownership stake in the Utah Jazz, joining majority owner and team governor Ryan Smith, and expressed a desire to take an active role in the franchise. D. Wade made good on his promise. He could be seen courtside throughout the season; he took action when an unsettling fan incident went down during the postseason, and he became a mentor to then-Jazz star Donovan Mitchell.

The former Miami Heat star also added to his portfolio with something a bit closer to home. Wade, a Chicago native, joined the ownership group of the WNBA's Chicago Sky.

"It's a great opportunity to be a part of the league in its very early stages. ... Growth is going to happen, and so I want to be a part of the growth of this league," Wade said.

Kevin Durant -- Philadelphia Union, NJ/NY Gotham FC

In June 2020, Brooklyn Nets star Kevin Durant purchased a 5% stake in MLS' Philadelphia Union, and he has an option to purchase an additional 5% at a later date. Durant also had engaged in talks about purchasing part of D.C. United the year prior, but he said the discussion never progressed.

Durant expanded his portfolio in May of this year, after being named as a minority owner of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) club NJ/NY Gotham FC.

Thirty Five Ventures (35V), a company co-founded by the two-time NBA champion and entrepreneur Rich Kleiman, made a significant investment to acquire a stake in the club, marking the company's second investment in a professional soccer team.

Renee Montgomery -- Atlanta Dream

Former Atlanta Dream guard Renee Montgomery made history in February as part of a three-member investor group that was approved to purchase the team. Montgomery is the first former player to become both an owner and executive of a WNBA franchise. The ownership change followed pressure on former Republican Sen. Kelly Loeffler to sell her share of the Dream, after she angered WNBA players with her opposition to the league's racial justice initiatives.

Patrick Mahomes -- Kansas City Royals

Patrick Mahomes is no stranger to winning. While the Kansas City Royals can't exactly say the same, you can't rule out that the quarterback's winning ways might rub off on the franchise now that he is part of their ownership group. If Mahomes' status as an icon in Kansas City was in question (it wasn't), this move surely cemented it. Becoming a baseball owner made sense on several levels for the Chiefs' QB1. Not only was Mahomes -- who played baseball in college -- a legitimate pro prospect, his father, Pat Mahomes, spent 11 seasons in Major League Baseball. He also had to find some way to put that $503 million contract extension to good use.

Venus and Serena Williams -- Miami Dolphins, Angel City FC

Winning major titles and making history, that's what the Williams sisters do. In 2009, Venus and Serena became the first Black female minority owners in the NFL by purchasing a part of the Miami Dolphins. Musicians Jimmy Buffett, Gloria and Emilio Estefan, Fergie and Marc Anthony also bought shares in the team -- the Dolphins' ownership group is nothing if not eclectic. Then, last year, Serena Williams became part of the star-studded Angel City FC ownership group bringing a NWSL team to Los Angeles in 2022.

Mia Hamm, Abby Wambach and Julie Foudy -- Angel City FC

When Angel City FC arrived on the scene it did so in style. Before we even knew the Los Angeles based NWSL club's name, we knew it had superstar backing like no other. Among the 14 former USWNT players who are part of the group are Mia Hamm, Abby Wambach and Julie Foudy. I would have named Lauren Holiday, Shannon Boxx, Rachel Buehler, Amanda Cromwell, Joy Fawcett, Tisha Venturini Hoch, Angela Hucles, Shannon MacMillan, Saskia Webber and sisters Lorrie Fair Allen and Ronnie Fair Sullins, but I was really trying to stay true to my whole "I'm only going to name 20 athletes" thing from the intro. There are also a bunch of celebrities in the mix, but we don't have that kind of time.

Michael Jordan -- Charlotte Hornets

While we're on the subject of owners who haven't had the type of success we grew accustomed to in their playing days, I would be remiss if I didn't mention the GOAT. In 2010, Michael Jordan became the first ex-player to be a majority owner in the league when the NBA's Board of Governors unanimously approved his $275 million bid to buy the then Charlotte Bobcats in his home state of North Carolina. After a decade of underwhelming years, things look to be on the up for the now Hornets with Rookie of the Year LaMelo Ball providing a long-awaited spark in the organization. Never forget when his dad said he could beat MJ one-on-one ... good times.

Alex Rodriguez -- Minnesota Timberwolves, Minnesota Lynx

I don't know what part of this purchase feels less ideal to me, that Alex Rodriguez and his 50-50 business partner Marc Lore are only pursuing acquiring the Minnesota Timberwolves and Lynx after their original plan to buy the New York Mets failed or that Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards had no idea who former MLB star A-Rod was. Either way, the $1.5 billion deal is expected to close around July 1.

David Beckham -- Inter Miami

David Beckham, iconic soccer player and remains-to-be-seen owner. Beckham -- who is incredibly hands on with the franchise -- is part of an ownership group which was initially called Miami Beckham United but now operates under the name Miami Freedom Park LLC. Beckham and Inter Miami have seemingly been riddled with controversy since the club's inception in 2018. But all those problems could be a thing of the past if Lionel Messi decides to head to MLS. Hey, stranger things have happened.

LeBron James -- Liverpool

Back in 2011, LeBron James and manager Maverick Carter became minority owners of Premier League club Liverpool after Fenway Sports Group, which purchased the team in 2010, became the sole marketer of James' global rights. The deal has turned out to be pretty lucrative for James -- his original stake in the club, valued at about $6.5 million, had grown to about $32 million as of 2018. In 2019, Liverpool won the Premier League for their first top-flight league title in thirty years.

James Harden -- Houston Dynamo, Houston Dash

James Harden might not be in Houston anymore, but the former Rockets superstar's presence is still felt in the city. The Beard purchased a 5% stake in the group that controls MLS' Houston Dynamo and NWSL's Houston Dash in 2019. Boxer Oscar De La Hoya is also part of the group. The Dash won their first NWSL title last year, so he's probably feeling pretty good about that investment.

Russell Wilson and Ken Griffey Jr. -- Seattle Sounders

What do Russell Wilson, Ken Griffey Jr. and Macklemore have in common? They are all part of the Seattle Sounders' ownership group. Wilson, along with his wife, musician Ciara, purchased a stake in the team in 2019 -- just in time for them to win an MLS Cup title. Griffey Jr. and his family followed suit in November 2020.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic -- Hammaraby

Seemingly everything Zlatan does makes people react intensely, and that remained true when he purchased part of Swedish team Hammaraby back in 2019. Fans of Malmo, another Swedish team where Zlatan started his professional career, reacted by vandalizing a statue of Zlatan outside the team's home stadium, placing a toilet seat around one of its arms.

Magic Johnson -- Los Angeles Dodgers

Big LA guy. In 2012, Lakers great Magic Johnson was part of a group that bought the Los Angeles Dodgers from Frank McCourt for a record $2 billion. At the time, the price shattered the mark for a sports franchise. Magic kept it real at the time of purchase when explaining his role in recruiting free agents, saying that while he can't talk hitting or pitching with players, he "can talk winning." If recent history is any indication (in case you blacked out all of 2020 -- the Dodgers won the World Series), it worked.

stories.headline: Kangaroos bounce Kiwis for fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup title
stories.summary: The Kangaroos have won a fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup, toppling New Zealand 32-12 in Brisbane.
stories.body:
The Kangaroos have punished a disappointing New Zealand, with Reece Walsh running riot in a 32-12 World Cup final waltz.

There was an expectation the Kiwis, searching for their second Cup title and first since 2008, would push Australia all the way after a two-point loss in a pulsating tournament opener.

But the visitors struggled from the outset in Brisbane on Sunday night, Jamayne Isaako's kick-off floating long in a sign of things to come.

Walsh dazzled at fullback for the Kangaroos, his pace, vision and wicked footwork too much as he helped lay on two tries and generally wreak havoc around the ruck and close to the line.

Conversely, Walsh's New Zealand opposite Kalyn Ponga -- International Rugby League's Golden Boot winner on Thursday night -- was unable to get into game.

Australian hooker Harry Grant and halves Tom Dearden and Cam Munster completely outplayed their error-riddled opposites, while the Kangaroos' pack muscled up.

Dearden laid on two first-half tries for Liam Martin with well-timed short balls, while Bradman Best was rewarded for an inspired chase-down tackle of Jahrome Hughes with a try soon after.

When Tom Trbojevic scored to begin the second half it was 28-6 and effectively game over.

Jack Bostock completed his breakout season with a try in each half for Australia.

It was the Kangaroos' fourth consecutive title and 10th in the last 11 tournaments, dating back to 1975.

stories.headline: VAR review: Explaining Yoro's early red card in Man United-Liverpool clash
stories.summary: VAR often causes controversy, but how are decisions made? Our resident ref, Andy Davies, explains all.
stories.body:
The video assistant referee causes controversy every week, whether it be the Premier League, Champions League or FA Cup, but how are those decisions made and are they correct?

For the 2026-27 season, we are taking a look at the major incidents to explain the process in terms of both VAR protocol and the laws of the game. The most surprising, controversial and complicated decisions will be examined all season long right here.

Photo credit: USA Sports, NBC

Andy Davies (@andydaviesref) is a former Select Group referee, with over 12 seasons on the elite list, working across the Premier League and Championship. With extensive experience at the elite level, he has operated within the VAR space in the Premier League and offers a unique insight into the processes, rationale and protocols that are delivered on a matchday.

Yoro red card vs. Liverpool in Pochettino deubt

Liverpool vs. Man United (Nov. 22)
Referee: Sam Barrott

VAR: John Brooks

Time: 8 minutes

Incident: Manchester United defender Leny Yoro sent off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity (DOGSO).

What Happened: Liverpool striker Alexander Isak latched onto a forward ball and was bundled over by a clumsy challenge from Yoro. Referee Barrott was quick to send Yoro off for denying an obvious goal scoring opportunity.

VAR Decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of a red card.

VAR Review: VAR ref Brooks didn't need long to check and clear the on-field decision. It was as straight forward a check you would want as a VAR.

Verdict / Insight: A straightforward decision for referee Barrott to send Yoro off for DOGSO after eight mins as the contact between him and Isak was clear.

In DOGSO situations such as this one, the referee must quickly determine if the ball is with playing distance when the foul contact occurs from the defender, which was the case in this incident.

Such a key decision like this one, so early and obvious, would have settled any nervous energy that Barrott would have been managing in the early stages of this match. In big ticket games, any key decisions have enormous consequences. However, Yoro made this easy situation for the referee to deal with.

This was a correct decision and a positive process from the referee.

Haaland goal vs. Fulham ruled out

Man City 1-1 Fulham (Nov. 21)
Referee: Tom Bramall

VAR: James Bell

Time: 24 minutes

Incident: Man City's Erling Haaland disallowed goal for foul on Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno.

What Happened: Haaland managed to get on the end of a deep cross, directing the ball into arms of Leno. However, the Fulham goalkeeper appeared to spill the ball, and Haaland followed up his original effort and bundled the ball into the net. Referee Bramall disallowed the goal as he felt Leno had control of the ball, awarding a foul to Fulham.

VAR Decision: No goal, stuck with the referee's on-field decision.

VAR Review: A debatable outcome, where there is no conclusive evidence to prove the on-field decision incorrect, and therefore this is not an incident VAR would intervene on.

Verdict / Insight: By the laws of the game, the goalkeeper only needs to have one hand engaged with the ball for it to be deemed to be under his control.

Referee Tom Bramall had a poor view of the challenge and its circumstance. In truth, he would have used a level of experience and guesswork to reach his outcome of disallowing the goal, and it would have felt the best outcome in the moment -- I would have given the same!

However, whilst I have seen some "still" images that possibly show the goalkeeper's hands near the ball, replays show a slightly different picture where the ball looked to have been spilt by the Fulham goalkeeper and equally his immediate body language in real-time and before he had time to think for a second, told a story of a player who had made an error.

Ultimately, Fulham's Leno can think himself fortunate that this one fell his way and City can be aggrieved; it's a decision that could have fallen either way in real time.

Did Lammens interfere with Suzuki?
Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa (Nov. 8)
Referee: Chris Kavanagh

VAR: Craig Pawson

Time: 96 minutes

Incident: Possible foul in Manchester United's equalizing goal.

What happened: Bruno Fernandes swung in a last-chance corner kick as Man United threw every player they had on the pitch, including keeper Senne Lammens, into the penalty area at 4-3 down.

Patrick Dorgu outjumped the Aston Villa defenders and, with keeper Zion Suzuki flapping at the ball, nodded home what seemed like a straightforward header into the net. However, Suzuki believed he was fouled by opposite number Lammens as the United No. 1 attempted to block the Villa keeper. Lammens made contact with Suzuki while neither looking at the ball nor making any attempt to play it.

Referee Kavanagh was unmoved by the appeals, yellow-carding Suzuki for his protests and awarding the goal.

VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of goal.

VAR review: VAR checked the incident and was comfortable that although Lammens clearly had intent to disturb Suzuki from having a clear path to punch the ball away by bumping into him, any contact was minimal and, more importantly, his impact on the Villa keeper was a 50-50 call.

This is a ratio where VAR is not keen to get involved and will stick with the on-field decision.

Verdict: Even prominent Man United fan Mark Goldbridge was sure that VAR should have got involved. But I believe the VAR was correct not to intervene in this situation as it fell short of the threshold for a clear on-field error.

Though Lammens' intention was obvious, intent is not a punishable offense, and the many replays didn't show enough of an impactful physical action on Suzuki that met the criteria for an intervention. However, Lammens did gamble with this play, and if referee Kavanagh had judged his action differently and awarded a late free kick to Villa, United could have few complaints.

This was a borderline call either way, and I am comfortable that the on-field decision should stick regardless of which way it fell.

Arsenal robbed of a penalty
Arsenal 1-0 Hull City (Nov. 7)
Referee: Farai Hallam

VAR: Michael Oliver

Time: 42 minutes

Incident: Penalty not awarded to Arsenal for an offside offense.

What happened: Hull's Nobel Mendy appeared to grab the shirt of Kai Havertz as the Arsenal attacker attempted to get on the end of a ball into the box.

In a confusing twist and following a VAR review, Hallam explained to the stadium that a foul action had been committed by Mendy, but Havertz was in an offside position and therefore the decision was no penalty and a restart of an indirect free kick to Hull.

VAR decision: VAR recommended an on-field review for a possible penalty to Arsenal.

VAR review: Oliver asked Hallam to review the possible penalty to Arsenal at the pitchside monitor. Once at the screen, Hallam agreed that a foul had been committed by Mendy on Havertz, however he also determined that Havertz was in an offside position when the ball was played and therefore the outcome should be a defensive free kick to Hull and not a penalty to Arsenal.

Verdict: In a complex and confusing set of circumstances, the law was incorrectly applied in this incident by Hallam. A penalty should have been the outcome, and fortunately for him and ProRef, Arsenal went on to win the game, which will dampen any fallout from the situation.

What the law says: If a player in an offside position is fouled before or without committing an offside offense, the foul is to be penalized.

I have some sympathy for Hallam, as the judgment of when a player should be judged as impacting an opponent can be open to interpretation. The positioning of Havertz and the possibility of him impacting on Mendy's next action has clearly caused a misread of the situation with the referee applying the law incorrectly.

Between the referee, Oliver and his assistant VAR, the correct outcome should have been reached, and the "live comms" will be interesting when they are released. I have been a big advocate of "live comms" being available, and this is another incident when some much-needed clarity was needed in real time, which could easily have been communicated and explained.

Liverpool denied a penalty in close game?

Liverpool vs. Arsenal

Referee: Andy Madley

VAR: Stuart Attwell

Time: 34 mins

Incident: Possible penalty to Liverpool

What happened: A cross into the Arsenal penalty was nearly headed toward goal by Alexander Isak, but it appeared that he was having his shirt pulled by Jurriën Timber. Referee Andy Madley was unmoved and play continued.

VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of no penalty.

VAR review: An interesting incident for VAR to check. However, once reviewed they felt the contact fell short of a clear on-field error and cleared the decision.

Verdict: This incident will be a major talking point, and Liverpool can feel aggrieved that there was no intervention by VAR for this holding offense by Timber. In real time it looked like a foul act by Timber; however, it would have been difficult for Madley to be sure how impactful the contact was from his position at pitch level, and so a non-decision in the moment is understandable.

This season, VAR has been encouraged to set a high bar and not intervene unless an on-field decision is clearly incorrect. The man in the hub on this occasion, Stuart Attwell, clearly felt this fell short of this threshold. However, when analyzing the incident, the action by Timber was deliberate; he made no attempt to play the ball and acted with the sole motivation of impacting Isak's ability to head the ball toward goal, in which he succeeded.

When such a deliberate action has a direct impact on an opponent's ability to play the ball, this must be penalized. In my opinion, Attwell fell short of his responsibilities by not recommending an on-field review and this will go down as an error by VAR in a key Premier League match.

Did Lisandro Martinez deserve a red card?

Chelsea 2-0 Manchester United (Oct. 31)
Referee: Peter Bankes

VAR: James Bell

Time: 61 minutes

Incident: Chelsea were awarded a penalty following a VAR on-field review, and Lisandro Martínez was sent off for committing a second yellow card offense.

What happened: Man United defender Lisandro Martínez seemed to lead with his arm, contacting with the head of Chelsea's Wesley Fofana with an aerial challenge.

VAR decision: VAR recommended an on-field review for a possible penalty following the reckless challenge by Martínez on Fofana.

VAR review: With no decision on the field by referee Bankes, VAR felt uncomfortable with this challenge but could only intervene if he felt the referee had made a clear error.

Following several replays, the VAR felt that the challenge met the criteria for a clear foul and a missed incident by the referee, explaining that Martínez's act was clearly late, made no attempt to play the ball as he was facing his opponent and not the ball. And, most importantly, that the contact with his arm was a reckless action.

VAR recommended that the referee reviewed the challenge at the pitchside screen. Once at the monitor, the referee agreed with his VAR, awarded the penalty and issued a second yellow card to Martínez and sent him off.

Verdict: A correct intervention from VAR with a penalty and a second yellow card for Martínez the right outcome.

The challenge by Martínez was a poor one; by leading with his arm when making an aerial challenge and connecting with an opponent, there was always a very high chance that a yellow card would follow.

It was surprising that referee Bankes did not award the penalty in real-time, as the reckless contact by Martínez looked clear on first sight. On reflection, he'll be disappointed.

However, credit to the VAR. With the emphasis this season on minimal interventions and the pressure that surrounds their every action, it was a positive decision to recognize that this clear error needed correcting.

Why was Matheus Cunha's goal disallowed?

Time: 34 minutes

Incident: Man United's Matheus Cunha had a goal disallowed for offside.

What happened: A deep Man United corner was headed back across goal by Harry Maguire and nudged into the back of the net by Cunha. However, following a quick VAR check, Cunha was deemed to be in an offside position and the goal was disallowed.

VAR decision: A factual decision to disallow the goal for an offside offence.

VAR review: A quick check with the use of the semi-automated system (SAOT) clearly showed that Cunha's left leg was in an offside position when the ball was played by teammate Maguire.

Verdict: Not a clear or easy decision to make in real time, however the goal was correctly disallowed with the use of SAOT as Cunha's leg strayed beyond the last defender when Maguire played the ball back across the box.

No need for an on-field review by the referee in this situation, as this was a factual decision.

Why did Man United's Heaven avoid red card for two-footed tackle?

Manchester United 0-3 Bournemouth (Oct. 25)

Referee: Jarred Gillett

VAR: Paul Howard

Time: 37 minutes

Incident: Possible red card for Manchester United's Ayden Heaven

What happened: United defender Heaven flew into a challenge on Bournemouth's Evanilson. His tackle looked dangerous -- it was over the top of ball and both feet off the ground. Referee Gillett issued a yellow card to the defender, with disgruntled Bournemouth players expecting the card to be red.

VAR decision: VAR agreed with the on-field decision of a yellow card and cleared the decision as correct.

VAR review: The on-field communication from Gillett would have guided the VAR into a non-intervention as the description of the challenge was accurate to the replays reviewed.

Only a clear error or a complete misread of the challenge would have instigated an on-field review from the VAR. The referee described the challenge as reckless, showing a disregard for the safety of his opponent, and the VAR agreed with this reading of the incident and a yellow card outcome.

Verdict and insight: A correct outcome on-field and non-intervention by VAR; this challenge did not meet the threshold for a red card for a Serious Foul Play (SFP) tackle.

While an area of judgment, the tipping point between red and yellow card outcomes is normally based around level of contact on an opponent. The action by Heaven did tick some of the SFP boxes when considering a sanction, however the fact that there was no contact or any real danger to Evanilson, met a yellow criteria card.

It showed a disregard for an opponent's safety by his recklessness, but nothing more.

Should Brentford's Yarmoliuk have been sent off?
Brentford 1-2 Liverpool (Oct. 17)
Referee: John Brooks

VAR: Darren England

Time: 45 + 3 minutes

Incident: Brentford defender Yehor Yarmoliuk sent off for violent conduct.

What happened: With Liverpool setting up for a corner kick and time ticking away at the end of the first half, Brentford defender Yarmoliuk and Liverpool's Jérémy Jacquet clashed, with the Liverpool player ending up on the floor.

Following a lengthy VAR review, referee Brooks agreed with the VAR recommendation and finally sent Yarmoliuk off for committing a violent action and headbutting Jacquet.

VAR decision: VAR overturn. Red Card for violent conduct.

VAR review: England took time to recommend an on-field review, as Yarmoliuk's violent action wasn't conclusive from all replay angles. However, the penalty-area tight camera eventually gave him the clear evidence he needed to ask John Brooks to visit the pitch-side monitor and review the incident.

Verdict and insight: A correct VAR intervention in this incident, with Brentford's Yarmoliuk committing a violent action towards his opponent and the red card an expected outcome.

Like Rodrigo Bentancur's red card for Spurs in the last match round, when a player deliberately heads at an opponent and makes contact, it is very likely to end in a red card.

The four minutes it took VAR to reach the point of an on-field review is frustrating, as this should have been cleared up a lot quicker -- this will be something ProRef will need to improve moving forward.

Additionally, some discussion as to why the restart was not a penalty kick, considering it was a defender committing an offense on an attacker in the penalty area. However, the ball was not in play when the incident occurred and therefore the original corner restart was correct.

Was Gravenberch wrongly sent off in Liverpool-Man City?
Liverpool 0-3 Man City (Oct. 11)
Referee: Chris Kavanagh

VAR: Paul Howard

Time: 62 minutes

Incident: Liverpool's Ryan Gravenberch sent off for a second yellow card at a key stage in the match

What happened: Having already received a yellow card early in the match, Gravenberch fouled City's Jérémy Doku and received a second yellow card from Kavanagh.

VAR review: Newly introduced into the Premier League this season, second yellow cards can now be reviewed by VAR, but only if they are factually incorrect, and this situation does not fit this category.

Verdict and insight: Most won't like this second yellow card decision, and it will be viewed as "soft." However, Kavanagh was put into a difficult position by Gravenberch's late, clumsy challenge on Doku, which clearly denied the Man City attacker a promising attack as he had clear opportunity to attack Liverpool in a positive area of the pitch. The subsequent yellow card was not a surprise.

These situations are the worst type of situations for referees, because you really want a second-card offense to be undebatable and obvious to everyone. Technical offenses can be questioned and heavily debated, regardless of whether the referee is correct in law.

Gravenberch can feel aggrieved by his first yellow card. From the replays, it looks like the referee misjudged the contact made by the Liverpool midfielder on Elliot Anderson, and on reflection, a free kick alone would have been a better outcome. However, once a player is on a yellow card and challenges an opponent from behind, as Gravenberch did on Doku, the player is running a very high risk of receiving a second yellow if the challenge is a foul and has consequence.

Liverpool will feel hard done by, but the second yellow card was a correct call from the referee.

Should Man United have gotten a penalty at Fulham?
Fulham 1-1 Man United (Sept. 20)
Referee: Peter Bankes

VAR: Nick Hopton

Time: 86 minutes

Incident: Possible penalty to Man United for a handball

What happened: Man United's Lisandro Martínez felt he should have earned a penalty when he fired the ball at Fulham defender Calvin Bassey from close range and the ball struck Bassey's arm. The referee did not feel it was an offence and waved away the appeals for a penalty.

VAR decision: VAR agreed with the referee's interpretation of the incident, that the ball was struck at close range, defenders' arms were close to his body and within bodyline and therefore not a handball offence. VAR checked and cleared the on-filed decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: While Man United might have wanted the penalty, this was a correct on-field decision by the refereeing team and non-intervention by VAR.

This incident is a good example of how the handball law can create confusion in these types of situations. When the ball is struck at close range, the law is clear that the referee should allow play to continue if the player's hand or arm movement is the result of a natural reflex to potentially protect the player's face, and if such action does not make their body unnaturally bigger.

Additionally, if arms are within the body line and the ball would have struck the body/face this should also be taken into consideration when applying this law.

Bassey's reaction falls within this interpretation and was a good read by the on-field assistant referee, who would have led the communication in this incident.

Was Rice lucky not to be sent off at Brighton?
Brighton & Hove Albion 3-0 Arsenal (Sept. 19)
Referee: Darren England

VAR: Tim Wood

Time: 90 + 7 mins

Incident: Possible red card for Arsenal's Declan Rice

What happened: Rice picked up a late yellow card when he appeared to kick out at Brighton's Malick Yalcouyé in an off-the-ball incident.

VAR decision: The on-field decision of yellow card was checked and cleared as correct by the VAR.

In these types of situations, VAR involvement can be triggered only if they believe the on-field refereeing team missed a violent act or an act or brutality. VAR was comfortable that the action by Rice did not meet either threshold, so the check was a straightforward one.

Verdict: This frustrated act by Rice was picked up in real time by the fourth official and certainly high risk, when considering many off-the-ball, non-footballing offenses are often interpreted as a red card offense by referees and matched by the expectations of football, so Rice can consider himself fortunate. However, I am comfortable that this action in isolation was a frustrated and petulant attempt at a trip on Yalcouyé and not a violent act or act of brutality, therefore a yellow card feels like a correct and sensible outcome.

VAR would never get involved in this situation unless there was clear evidence that the on-field outcome was incorrect, so the yellow card was correctly checked and cleared. Rice is very fortunate that the original on-field interpretation of his action was only a yellow card, otherwise he would be serving a three-game ban following the international break.

Why was Phil Foden sent off in the Manchester derby?

Manchester United 0-1 Manchester City (Sept. 13)

Referee: Michael Oliver

VAR: Matt Donohue

Time: 23rd minute

Incident: Red card for Phil Foden of Manchester City

What happened: City's Foden appeared to kick out at United's Bruno Fernandes following an untidy tangle between the two players.

VAR decision: The VAR checked and confirmed the red card for violent conduct by Foden as a correct decision.

VAR review: The VAR had a straightforward check to confirm this on-field decision, as there was a clear kick out from Foden into Fernandes' body. The pictures aligned with the on-field comms from referee Michael Oliver, and this was a simple VAR process.

Verdict: Foden can have no complaints as he lost his composure in this situation.

There might be some debate around the level of contact of Foden's action. However, when you kick out in nature that Foden did in this moment, it is very likely that a red card for violent card will be the outcome, regardless of level of contact.

Referee Oliver was very quick with his decision, but his positioning was excellent, allowing him all the available information to reach his outcome. Additionally, it was a straightforward review for the VAR, and he correctly checked and cleared the decision having considered all the dynamics of the incident.

Why was Enzo Fernández not ruled offside in Man City's goal?
Manchester United 0-1 Manchester City (Sept. 13)
Time: 60th minute

Incident: City awarded controversial winning goal

What happened: Erling Haaland scored what looked like a goal that would be disallowed for offside. However, following a long VAR check, the goal was awarded and City took a significant lead.

VAR decision: The VAR overturned the on-field decision and awarded a goal, judging that Haaland was onside before he tapped into the United net.

VAR review: There were two key elements in this offside goal review. First, semi-automated technology showed that Haaland was in an onside position when the ball was crossed by his teammate. Second, the VAR had a subjective decision to make; did Man City's Enzo Fernández either play the ball or impact on Man United center back Lisandro Martínez's ability to play the ball given that Fernández was in an offside position and in front of the goal?

The VAR was comfortable that Fernández didn't meet any of the offside criteria and advised the referee that a goal should be the outcome.

Verdict: This was an incorrect decision by the VAR to award a goal to City, a controversial outcome that will create a lot of noise in the coming days.

What was correct: the factual aspect of the decision, which showed that Haaland was onside when the cross was played. Technology is now applied in these situations, and pictures clearly showed the position of the City attacker behind the leg of United's Dorgu.

However, the subjective element of this decision is where the VAR has made his error. There are two significant sections of law that the VAR did not apply in this moment, which should have resulted in a different outcome and the goal disallowed. It should be deemed an offside offense when (A) A player clearly attempts to play a ball that is close when this action impacts an opponent, or (B) A player makes an obvious action that clearly impacts the ability of an opponent to play the ball.

In this situation, Man United's Martinez was clearly impacted by the position and action of Fernández. Martinez's ability to defend the ball was certainly affected by Fernández, and this should have been recognized within the VAR review.

The process in this situation should have been an on-field review, when the referee comes across to the screen and views the incident himself. This would have been a subjective decision and therefore only the referee can make the final decision.

Soccer doesn't like what it doesn't understand, and this was a confusing situation for everyone. The incident will be viewed as a big error and ultimately game-changing.

Should Sunderland have been given a penalty vs. Arsenal?

Sunderland 0-2 Arsenal (Sept. 12)

Referee: John Brooks

VAR: Stuart Attwell

Time: 54 min

Incident: Penalty awarded to Sunderland

What happened: With the score 0-0 early in the second half, Arsenal were left frustrated as defender Ezri Konsa was adjudged to have fouled Sunderland's Dan Ballard after a Sunderland corner, and referee John Brooks pointed to the spot.

VAR decision: VAR checked and confirmed the on-field decision of a penalty kick to Sunderland.

VAR review: Brooks' live comms described Konsa's actions on Ballard as being "all over him at the near post, facing the wrong way." Having considered the communication from the referee, VAR ruled that he was accurate in his description and his rationale for awarding a penalty kick, and confirmed the decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: With the heightened profile, focus, and referees asked to be more assertive in set-play situations such as corners, there was a high chance that a small number of penalty kicks would be awarded incorrectly, and this was an example of it playing out in real-time.

From the referee's on-field position, this incident would have looked like Konsa was clumsy with his contact on Ballard. As both players fall to the ground, referee Brooks believed that it was the Arsenal player who was pulling, deliberately facing away from the ball and committing a holding offense -- the type of foul the football world was hoping would be penalized this season.

However, from the replays, it was clear that though Arsenal's Konsa engaged with Ballard with normal contact, Ballard using his left arm to pull Konsa's shirt made the Arsenal defender spin and land on the Sunderland center back. Any punishable offense was, in fact, committed by Ballard and the restart should have been a defensive free kick.

Mikel Arteta was fuming afterwards and it's difficult to understand why VAR did not intervene in this situation given the information available to him, as it was a clear but understandable on-field error by the referee -- the referee's live description of the incident did not match the replay pictures, and this should be a red flag to the VAR.

This was a poor non-intervention by VAR, and an on-field review should have been recommended.

Why was Forest's Williams denied a winner vs. Spurs?
Nottingham Forest 0-0 Tottenham (Sep. 5)
Referee: Craig Pawson

VAR: Peter Bankes

Time: 67 min

Incident: Possible handball to Forest

What happened: Forest defender Neco Williams thought he had given his team the lead as he bundled it across the Spurs goal line. However, VAR overturned the goal for a handball offense.

VAR decision: VAR checked the referee's call of a goal for Forest and determined that Williams handled the ball immediately before scoring and recommended that the goal be disallowed.

VAR review: This was a difficult review for the VAR, which involved multiple angles and replay speeds to determine if this goal should be allowed to stand.

VAR Bankes would have been uncomfortable with the way Williams bundled the ball into the goal, as there was very high chance that it had struck his arm. However, even if the contact was accidental, the law states that any touch of the arm by the goalscorer immediately before a goal must be disallowed.

The in-goal camera provided the decisive information, as it showed the ball striking the arm of Williams as he threw himself in to try and score, creating a change in trajectory of the ball and resulting in a goal -- VAR recommended to the referee that he should disallow the goal for a handball.

Verdict and insight: Not an easy process for the VAR to review. However, once you see the decisive replays from inside Spurs' goal, it is a straightforward decision for the VAR, as the law dictates the outcome.

With so much debate surrounding the Harry Maguire "handball goal" from last week -- when the ball struck the arm of Maguire before his shot was deflected into the goal off a defender, meaning Maguire was not the actual scorer -- this scenario is far clearer and the correct outcome is reached.

How new standards cost Arsenal a clear penalty
Aston Villa 0-1 Arsenal (Aug. 31)
Referee: Jarred Gillett

VAR: James Bell

Time: 90 + 9 mins

Incident: Possible penalty to Arsenal

What happened: Arsenal's Bruno Guimarães was screaming for a penalty after he was challenged from behind by Villa's Ian Maatsen inside the box. Referee Jarred Gillett waved away the appeals.

VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of no penalty.

VAR review: VAR James Bell clearly applied the new "high bar" for intervention when he cleared this decision, taking the view that the referee's on-field decision not to award a penalty to Arsenal was not a clear and obvious error. After reviewing the replays, VAR quickly checked and cleared the decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: For me, this was a clear penalty kick that should've been awarded to Arsenal. I was surprised it was not given on-field by match referee Gillett, and equally surprised the VAR did not recommend a pitch-side review.

The decision by Villa's Maatsen to challenge in the nature he did, from behind with a scissor action and no opportunity to play the ball was a poor one. By making contact only with Guimarães and none on the ball, there can be little doubt that it met the threshold for a foul -- and it took place inside the penalty box.

The surprising non-intervention by VAR is a result of the Premier League's desire this season to have less involvement and only very clear errors to be corrected, with a new "higher bar" for interventions to be applied.

It's a positive principle that should result in less time spent re-litigating decisions, yes. However, this was clearly a mistake from the on-field referee not to award a penalty and, in my opinion, this was an intervention that has been missed by the VAR team.

Arsenal winning the game will cover the narrative to some degree, however, if this was a deciding moment that cost Arsenal all three points, the profile of the incident would've been significant.

The high bar will absolutely improve the game and lower the expectations from football that VAR should get involved in everything, however it is so important that clear fouls in the penalty area, like this situation, do not get overlooked when the referee has mis-read a key moment.

Why did Maguire's obvious handball not cancel goal?
Manchester United 5-2 Ipswich Town (Aug. 30)
Referee: Craig Pawson

VAR: Jarred Gillett

Time: 56th minute

Incident: Possible handball in lead-up to Man United's second goal by Harry Maguire

What happened: The ball was cleared out of Ipswich's box toward Maguire, and the ball appeared to strike the arm of Maguire. He brought the ball to his feet and struck the ball toward goal, where it then took a grave deflection from Ipswich defender Jacob Greaves before going into the goal. Following a VAR review, the goal was allowed to stand.

VAR decision and communications: The referee's call of goal for Manchester United was checked and confirmed by VAR, who deemed that Maguire was not the immediate goalscorer after an accidental handball.

VAR: "It's an own goal and the accidental handball is not punishable, so we recommend you award the goal."

VAR review: With the knowledge that the ball had clearly struck the arm of Maguire, the VAR had two key elements to consider:

(1) Was Maguire's shot on target before it struck Greaves and entered the goal? In other words: was Maguire the goalscorer?

(2) Was the handball by Maguire accidental or a punishable as an intentional handball offence?

The answers to both questions could have resulted in a different outcome, but the VAR determined that it was clearly an own goal by Greaves, meaning Maguire was not the scorer, and that the handball incident was accidental. Both details meant the ball striking the arm of Maguire was negated in law, and the VAR recommended to the referee that the goal should be awarded.

Verdict and insight: It's understandable that Ipswich Town will feel hard-done by the decision.

If Maguire had scored the goal, then his handling of the ball in the lead-up would've canceled out the goal. It's only because it took the massive deflection that changed the trajectory of the ball that Maguire's incidental handball did not result in the goal being overturned.

In truth, it was a 50/50 decision that could have fallen the other way if the judgement of VAR was a different one. But the law doesn't allow a goal to be disallowed in this situation if the handball by Maguire was judged as accidental.

The subjective nature of handball in general is a confusing element of the game, and if VAR had judged this as a punishable handball and disallowed the goal, it would certainly have been a credible outcome given the context of the situation in my opinion -- and a more comfortable outcome for football.

However, the judgement by VAR Jared Gillett was not an incorrect one, with Maguire challenging for a bouncing ball and his arms in front of his body, the ball striking his left arm can certainly be deemed as accidental. It was on this occasion, with Man United the benefactor of it in this situation, and Ipswich rightfully feeling hard done by.

Should Liverpool have been bailed out by penalty?
Newcastle United 2-2 Liverpool (Aug. 23)
Referee: Stuart Attwell

VAR: James Bell

Time: 90 + 6 mins

Incident: Penalty awarded to Liverpool for a challenge by Lewis Hall on Victor Muñoz

What happened: Liverpool's Muñoz charged into the Newcastle penalty area late into the game, and Hall made a clumsy challenge bringing the Liverpool player to the ground. Referee Stuart Attwell pointed to the spot for a late penalty for the Reds.

VAR decision and communications: The referee's call of penalty for the challenge by Hall on Muñoz was checked and confirmed by VAR.

The referee: "He doesn't play the ball. He makes clear contact."

VAR: "It's knee into thigh contact. Confirming the on-field decision of penalty."

Verdict: This was a correct decision made by referee Atwell and his assistant, and a decision I felt was clear in real-time.

In this type of situation, with an attacker moving into the penalty area at speed with the ball under control, any challenge by a defender must successfully play the ball or they run a very high risk of committing a foul.

Hall was naïve to make his clumsy challenge in the manner he did, and Muñoz was too clever for the Newcastle defender. This was a clear foul by Hall, and a penalty kick a correct outcome.

While it may feel to Newcastle fans that Liverpool were bailed out and gifted a draw after middling performance, Hall's foul was needless and to blame for Liverpool equalizing.

stories.headline: Wembanyama makes history in 18 minutes, finishes game with 50 points
stories.summary: Victor Wembanyama had his third career 50-point outing during a win over the Pelicans to go along with 19 rebounds, five blocks and four steals.
stories.body:
SAN ANTONIO -- Victor Wembanyama overwhelmed the New Orleans Pelicans with his third career 50-point outing Saturday, when he also became the first player in the play-by-play era to tally at least 30 points, 10 rebounds, three blocks and three steals in a half, to lead the San Antonio Spurs to a 114-91 win.

Wembanyama had 32 points, 12 rebounds, three steals and three blocked shots in the first half, a stat line no other player has matched in an entire game this season.

He did that in nearly 18 minutes as the Spurs sent the Pelicans to their ninth loss in 10 games. The 22-year-old finished with 19 rebounds, five blocks and four steals and admitted to some stat padding after Spurs coach Mitch Johnson told him he had 1:30 left of playing time to reach 50 points.

"I told him it might be enough [time]," Wembanyama said.

He was correct. In 1:14 of the fourth quarter, Wembanyama drilled back-to-back 3-pointers to reach 50 points and give San Antonio a 108-82 lead. Wembanyama took a seat on the Spurs' bench between Luke Kornet and De'Aaron Fox 22 seconds later, when Johnson called a timeout to sub him out for rookie Tarris Reed Jr.

"I just want to keep stacking them up," Wembanyama said of his historic performances. "I don't plan on doing those. They just come when we play the right way as a team. Hopefully, there's many more coming."

Wembanyama tied LeBron James and Devin Booker for the second-most 50-point performances in NBA history by a player 22 or younger. Wembanyama joined Hall of Famer and former Spurs great David Robinson as the only players with multiple 50-point, five-block games in league history since blocks were tracked (1973-74).

Wembanyama is the first player to do it multiple times in the same season.

"He started the game off aggressive, and he was trying to play with a lot of force offensively, specifically in terms of taking up real estate, trying to get to the rim," Johnson said. "It's so interesting when people play like that, especially with his talent level. Then, it helps your rhythm with your shots and everything else. I was just hoping he got to 50 when he did. That would've been hard to take him out that close to 50."

Wembanyama notched his second career half with at least 30 points with near surgical precision. He hit 12 of 15 shots from the field, including 3 of 5 from 3-point range over the first two quarters.

With 2:30 remaining until intermission, Wembanyama had outscored New Orleans' starting five.

Reigning NBA Sixth Man of the Year Keldon Johnson perused the box score during the postgame news conference, taking in what he had just witnessed. With his eyes darting back and forth, Johnson started to rattle off Wembanyama's numbers.

"Vic had 50 tonight. That was impressive. [He shot] 20-for-29; that's crazy," Johnson said. "He had it rolling, and the main thing was if he's open or getting to his spots, make sure you give it to him. That's just the emphasis for everybody."

Actress and singer Selena Gomez sat courtside among the sellout crowd of 18,708 at Frost Bank Center, and Wembanyama made sure the longtime Spurs fan was entertained. Wembanyama glanced at Gomez in the first half to acknowledge her presence after he knocked down a corner 3.

"Of course," Wembanyama said, laughing. "I had to show out for Selena."

He even acknowledged postgame that the "ethical basketball" he espoused last season wasn't part of the equation or thought process at the end of a career night in which he forced up one last 3-pointer.

"Ethical basketball, there's not really a clearly defined term what it means," he said. "But for me, what it means is creating a culture as a team, taking the right shots, beating teams by having everybody on the floor as a threat for the opponent at all times. That step-back [3] to the right I took, it doesn't correlate with this. It didn't fit to the definition. Yeah, I did try to get a 3 up when I had 47 points."

Was he OK with breaking from the tenets he defines as ethical basketball?

"Yeah, of course," he said. "I made it, didn't I? I don't think Wilt [Chamberlain] thought about [stat padding] when he had 98 points. I don't think he thought about making the extra, extra pass. If he could've went for 100, he would've, and he did. I try to not think about it."

stories.headline: Champions League upstarts Como suffer Moise Kean injury blow
stories.summary: Como forward Moise Kean is set to be out injured for at least two months and could miss Champions League games against Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona.
stories.body:
Como forward Moise Kean is set to be out injured for at least two months, his coach Cesc Fabregas said on Friday, and could miss Champions League games against Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona.

The 26-year-old Italy forward injured his right leg against Belgium in the Nations League this week but the latest issue was with his left leg, Fabregas said.

- Meet Como's Nico Paz, the heir to Lionel Messi's No. 10 shirt for Argentina

- UCL talking points: First upsetting United, now NINE goals!? Are Como the real deal?

Como previously said Kean needed treatment on an injury in practice after returning from national team duty.

In its first season in the Champions League, Como have adapted stunningly fast with a 9-1 win at Lens and a pair of 4-1 victories at home to Manchester United and RB Leipzig.

Como are fourth in the 36-team standings ahead of hosting AEK Athens on Tuesday. The league phase for Como finishes with Real Betis next month and titleholders PSG, one of Kean's former clubs, and Barcelona in back-to-back weeks in January.

Kean arrived at Como on an initial season-long loan from Fiorentina and his injury leaves just Tasos Douvikas as a proven striker until the January transfer window. Kean has been limited to just four appearances for Como so far this season.

Como are fifth in Serie A and host Cagliari on Saturday.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.
